etymology: An English compound of hard + tack (an old word for food), so “hard food.” The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence is from 1830, in the United Service Magazine. It became the everyday ration of the Civil War soldier: a cracker of flour, water and salt that kept for a very long time.
biblical_def: Hardtack is a hard, dry cracker of flour, water and salt, baked to keep for months. During the Civil War it was one of the most common meals a soldier had. The men did not love it. The National Park Service records that they called it “sheet iron crackers” and “tooth duller,” and, when insects got into the boxes, “worm castles.” They softened it in coffee, broke it with a rifle butt into stew, or fried it in bacon fat. The Christian observation: hardtack is the bread of men far from home, eaten because it is what there is. Our Lord taught us to ask for exactly that much: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Mat 6:11). Israel learned the same lesson on manna in the wilderness, that God "suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna … that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only" (Deu 8:3). Paul, who knew hunger as well as plenty, wrote that he had learned "both to be full and to be hungry" (Php 4:12), and he called Timothy to "endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3). A soldier’s cracker is a fair picture of the Christian life: plain provision, received with thanks, on the way to a better table.
webster_summary: A hard, long-keeping cracker of flour, water and salt (OED earliest 1830); the Civil War soldier’s staple — a picture of daily bread received with thanks and hardness endured (Mat 6:11; 2Ti 2:3).
webster_full: HARDTACK, n. (from 1830, OED) A hard cracker or biscuit of flour, water and salt, baked to keep for long periods; ship’s and soldier’s bread. From hard + tack, food.
Civil War note: one of the most common soldier’s meals of the war (National Park Service, Manassas National Battlefield Park).
scriptures: Give us this day our daily bread.

And he humbled thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that he might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live.
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: An age of plenty forgets what hardtack taught: provision is daily, from God’s hand, and hardness is part of a soldier’s calling.
corruption_paragraphs: A generation that has never gone hungry tends to treat bread as owed rather than given. The petition “Give us this day our daily bread” becomes a formality, and complaint becomes the normal response to plain food. The soldiers who lived on hardtack grumbled too, but they ate it and marched.

Scripture does not praise hardship for its own sake, and it does not promise a soldier comfort. It calls him to contentment in abasing and abounding alike (Php 4:12) and to endure hardness for the sake of the One who enlisted him (2Ti 2:3).
roots_summary: hard + tack (food) → hardtack (OED earliest 1830) → Civil War soldier’s staple ration.
roots_lines: tack: an old English word for food or fare
1830: OED’s earliest evidence for hardtack, United Service Magazine
1861–1865: one of the most common meals of the Civil War soldier
usage: "The museum at Manassas still has a piece of Civil War hardtack."
Give us this day our daily bread. (Mat 6:11).
Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. (2Ti 2:3).

etymology: An English compound of dead + line. The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the word is from 1814, before the war. Its grim Civil War sense was the line in a military prison that a prisoner could not cross without being shot. The National Park Service notes that such deadlines were common in the open stockade prisons of the era, Andersonville among them, and not unique to it. The OED tags the word in fishing from the 1810s, in military use from the 1860s and in printing from the 1910s; the printing sense, the last moment copy could go to press, became today’s time limit.
biblical_def: A deadline today is the last moment by which something must be done. The word once meant something far worse. In the stockade prisons of the Civil War a low rail, a row of stakes or a rope marked the deadline, and a prisoner who crossed it could be shot by the guard. The National Park Service records deadlines at Andersonville, Camp Lawton, Camp Douglas, Florence, Rock Island and elsewhere. The Christian observation: every man lives inside a deadline he did not draw. Job confessed of man that God has "appointed his bounds that he cannot pass" (Job 14:5), and Hebrews states the line plainly: "it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Heb 9:27). The wise response is not dread but readiness: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12). The Gospel answers the last deadline with a present invitation: "behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2Co 6:2).
webster_summary: The last moment by which a thing must be done; once the line a Civil War prisoner could not cross without being shot (NPS). Every man lives within bounds God has appointed (Job 14:5; Heb 9:27).
webster_full: DEADLINE, n. (from 1814, OED) 1. In Civil War military prisons, a line, rail or row of stakes beyond which a prisoner might be shot. 2. (1910s, printing; OED) The latest time by which copy, work or a decision is due.
Correction note: the prison deadline is often treated as unique to Andersonville. The National Park Service shows it was common in stockade prisons of the era.
scriptures: Seeing his days are determined, the number of his months are with thee, thou hast appointed his bounds that he cannot pass;
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
(For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)
corruption_summary: A word born at a line of death now names a work due date; the deeper line, appointed by God, is the one the age forgets.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern life runs on deadlines, and most of them are small. The danger is that a man who meets every deadline at work ignores the one that cannot be moved. Scripture speaks of man’s days as determined and his bounds appointed (Job 14:5).
The answer is neither panic nor procrastination but redeeming the time, “because the days are evil” (Eph 5:16), and receiving the salvation God offers today (2Co 6:2).
roots_summary: dead + line (OED earliest 1814, fishing) → Civil War prison deadline (1860s) → printing due-time (1910s) → any time limit.
roots_lines: 1814: OED’s earliest evidence for deadline, in fishing
1860s: military sense (OED); the prison deadline, common in stockade prisons including Andersonville (NPS)
1910s: printing sense, the last moment copy can go to press (OED)
usage: "The Andersonville deadline was a low rail fence, and it was not the only one."
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. (Psa 90:12).
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment: (Heb 9:27).

etymology: An English compound of green + back. The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for the word is from before 1682, in the writing of Sir Thomas Browne. The money sense comes from the Civil War. The U.S. Currency Education Program records that in 1861 Congress authorized the Treasury to issue non-interest-bearing Demand Notes to finance the war, and that these notes earned the nickname “greenbacks” because of their color.
biblical_def: A greenback is a U.S. paper dollar. The name began with the Demand Notes of 1861, issued by the Treasury to pay for the Civil War and nicknamed for their green ink. In 1862 Congress added United States Notes, also called Legal Tender notes. The Christian observation: the greenback was war money, paper backed by the promise of a government at war. Our Lord, shown a coin, said "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s" (Mat 22:21). Money is lawful, and taxes are owed. But Scripture warns that money can become a master: "Ye cannot serve God and mammon" (Mat 6:24), and "the love of money is the root of all evil" (1Ti 6:10). It also binds the man who borrows, for "the borrower is servant to the lender" (Pro 22:7). And God requires honest measure from those who make and keep money: "Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD" (Pro 20:10).
webster_summary: A U.S. paper dollar, from the green Demand Notes of 1861 issued to finance the Civil War (U.S. Currency Education Program); money is to be rendered rightly, not served (Mat 22:21; Mat 6:24).
webster_full: GREENBACK, n. (word from before 1682, OED; money sense 1861) A U.S. paper note; originally the Treasury Demand Notes of 1861, nicknamed for their color.
1862: Congress authorized United States Notes (Legal Tender notes), red-sealed, circulating until 1971 (U.S. Currency Education Program).
scriptures: They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD.
corruption_summary: Money is a lawful tool and a ruinous master; the greenback, born of war debt, is a reminder that whoever serves money and borrows freely ends up a servant.
corruption_paragraphs: Paper money is a promise, and its worth depends on the honesty of those who issue it. Scripture condemns divers weights and divers measures (Pro 20:10), and the principle reaches every unjust scale.

For the household the warning is simpler. Money is to be rendered where it is owed (Mat 22:21), not loved (1Ti 6:10) and not served (Mat 6:24), and the family that lives on borrowing makes itself a servant to the lender (Pro 22:7).
roots_summary: green + back (OED earliest before 1682) → 1861 Treasury Demand Notes nicknamed “greenbacks” → any U.S. paper dollar.
roots_lines: Before 1682: OED’s earliest evidence for greenback (Sir Thomas Browne)
1861: Treasury Demand Notes issued to finance the Civil War, nicknamed “greenbacks” for their color
1862: United States Notes (Legal Tender notes) authorized; circulated until 1971
usage: "The first greenbacks were printed to pay for the Civil War."
They say unto him, Caesar’s. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. (Mat 22:21).
The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender. (Pro 22:7).

etymology: From carpet-bag, a traveling bag made of carpet, + -er. The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence for carpet-bagger is from 1868, in the London Daily News. Britannica describes it as a derogatory term first used during Reconstruction (1865–77) for a Northerner who moved to the South.
biblical_def: A carpetbagger was, in the speech of the postwar South, a Northerner who came south during Reconstruction. Britannica records that the word was applied to politicians and financial adventurers whom Southerners accused of coming south to use the newly enfranchised freedmen to obtain office or profit. The bag was the joke: a man who owned no more than he could carry. Today the word is used of any candidate who moves into a place to run for office there. The Christian observation: the word carries two lessons at once. Some newcomers did come for gain, and Scripture warns that "they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare" (1Ti 6:9). But the law of God also commanded Israel to love the stranger: "thou shalt love him as thyself" (Lev 19:34). A neighbor is to be judged by his conduct, not by where he came from: "Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment" (Joh 7:24).
webster_summary: A Northerner who moved South during Reconstruction (OED earliest 1868); now any outsider who moves in to seek office — to be judged by conduct, not origin (Joh 7:24; Lev 19:34).
webster_full: CARPETBAGGER, n. (from 1868, OED) 1. During Reconstruction (1865–77), a Northerner who moved to the South, especially one accused of seeking office or profit there (Britannica). 2. Any outsider who takes up residence in a place in order to run for office there.
scriptures: But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.
corruption_summary: A label for suspected motives became a label for anyone from elsewhere; Scripture condemns greed and also commands love for the stranger.
corruption_paragraphs: Every hard season produces men who come to profit from it, and the South after the war had its share. The temptation in the name, though, is to judge a man by his luggage. Scripture forbids judging by appearance (Joh 7:24).

Israel was told to love the stranger because Israel had been strangers in Egypt (Lev 19:34). The honest question about any newcomer is the one asked of every man: what does he do with what he is given?
roots_summary: carpet-bag + -er → carpet-bagger (OED earliest 1868) → Reconstruction-era Northerner in the South → any outsider seeking office.
roots_lines: carpet-bag: a traveling bag made of carpet
1865–77: Reconstruction; the term used of Northerners who moved South (Britannica)
1868: OED’s earliest evidence, London Daily News
usage: "The opposing campaign called him a carpetbagger because he had lived in the county less than a year."
Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment. (Joh 7:24).
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God. (Lev 19:34).

etymology: Of unknown origin, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which enters the word as scallywag. OED’s earliest evidence is from 1848, in John R. Bartlett’s dictionary, and it records the word in United States politics from the 1860s. Britannica describes the Reconstruction sense: a pejorative term for a white Southerner who supported the federal plan of Reconstruction.
biblical_def: A scalawag, in the politics of the postwar South, was a white Southerner who supported Reconstruction or joined the freedmen and the so-called carpetbaggers in backing Republican Party policies. Britannica notes that scalawags may have made up about 20 percent of the white electorate. Before the war the word was already a general insult for a worthless fellow, and in ordinary speech it still means a rascal. The Christian observation: scalawag was a word for a neighbor who had chosen the other side, and it was meant to wound. Our Lord warned against exactly that kind of speech: "whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council" (Mat 5:22). Paul told the church to put away "bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking" (Eph 4:31). A man may be wrong in his politics, but the case against him should be made with evidence, for "his neighbour cometh and searcheth him" (Pro 18:17).
webster_summary: A white Southerner who supported Reconstruction (Britannica); older, a rascal (OED, from 1848, origin unknown) — a name meant to wound a neighbor (Mat 5:22; Eph 4:31).
webster_full: SCALAWAG, n. (also scallywag; from 1848, OED) 1. A worthless fellow; a rascal. 2. During Reconstruction, a white Southerner who supported the federal plan of Reconstruction or the Republican Party (Britannica).
scriptures: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
corruption_summary: A name-calling word for a neighbor on the other side; Scripture forbids the contempt and requires that a man’s case be searched out honestly.
corruption_paragraphs: Political names are often made to end an argument rather than win it. Scalawag told a man that his neighbors no longer counted him as one of their own.
The Christian may oppose a policy without despising the man who holds it. Contemptuous names are forbidden (Mat 5:22), and every cause must be examined, not merely asserted (Pro 18:17).
roots_summary: Origin unknown; scallywag (OED earliest 1848) → Reconstruction sense, a white Southern Republican (1860s) → general sense, a rascal.
roots_lines: 1848: OED’s earliest evidence, John R. Bartlett’s dictionary
1860s: OED records the word in United States politics
1865–77: a Reconstruction-era insult for white Southerners who backed the Republican Party (Britannica)
usage: "Grandfather called the puppy a little scalawag after it dug up the garden."
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice: (Eph 4:31).
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him. (Pro 18:17).

etymology: Probably a compound of jay + hawker, per the Oxford English Dictionary, which hedges the derivation. OED’s earliest evidence is from 1860, in the Ashtabula Sentinel. The American Battlefield Trust notes that the term originated in the prewar Bleeding Kansas period and was used for pro-Union partisan fighters.
biblical_def: A jayhawker was a free-state or pro-Union guerrilla of the Kansas–Missouri border. The American Battlefield Trust explains that in Missouri and the other border states guerrilla fighters of either side were commonly called bushwhackers, while the pro-Union partisans were also known as jayhawkers, a name from the prewar Bleeding Kansas years. The name lives on in the University of Kansas Jayhawk. The Christian observation: the border war was a war of raids on farms and towns, often against men who were not soldiers at all. God’s law is plain: "Thou shalt not steal" (Exo 20:15). John the Baptist told the soldiers who came to him, "Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages" (Luk 3:14). And private revenge belongs to no man: "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19).
webster_summary: A pro-Union guerrilla of the Kansas–Missouri border (OED earliest 1860; American Battlefield Trust) — a war of raids that God’s law against theft and revenge condemns (Exo 20:15; Rom 12:19).
webster_full: JAYHAWKER, n. (from 1860, OED) A free-state or pro-Union guerrilla of the Kansas–Missouri border in the Bleeding Kansas period and the Civil War (American Battlefield Trust).
scriptures: And the soldiers likewise demanded of him, saying, And what shall we do? And he said unto them, Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Raiding in a righteous cause is still raiding; Scripture forbids theft, violence and private vengeance on either side of a border.
corruption_paragraphs: Both sides of the border war told themselves they were avenging the other side’s raids, and the raids went on for years.
Scripture breaks that cycle at the root. A soldier is to do violence to no man beyond his lawful duty (Luk 3:14), and vengeance belongs to God alone (Rom 12:19).
roots_summary: Probably jay + hawker (OED, hedged) → Bleeding Kansas free-state partisan → Civil War pro-Union guerrilla (OED earliest 1860).
roots_lines: 1854–1859: Bleeding Kansas; the term originates in this period (American Battlefield Trust)
1860: OED’s earliest evidence, Ashtabula Sentinel
1861–1865: pro-Union guerrillas of the border states
usage: "The jayhawkers and the bushwhackers burned farms on both sides of the state line."
Thou shalt not steal. (Exo 20:15).
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. (Rom 12:19).

etymology: A clipping of secession, per the Oxford English Dictionary. OED’s earliest evidence is from 1861, the first year of the war, in the Ohio Statesman.
biblical_def: Secesh is Civil War slang, a clipped form of secession, used for the secession cause and for those who backed it. The Oxford English Dictionary’s earliest evidence is from 1861, the first year of the war. The Christian observation: the word is short because it was said often and in anger, in towns where neighbors had taken different sides. Our Lord warned that "every city or house divided against itself shall not stand" (Mat 12:25). The goal set before God’s people is the opposite of division: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" (Psa 133:1). And the remedy for bitterness is the same in every age: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you" (Eph 4:31).
webster_summary: Civil War slang clipped from secession (OED earliest 1861) — a word of a divided house, which cannot stand (Mat 12:25; Psa 133:1).
webster_full: SECESH, n. & adj. (from 1861, OED) Secession; a secessionist; secessionist. Clipped from secession.
scriptures: And Jesus knew their thoughts, and said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand:
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
corruption_summary: A clipped insult from a divided country; Scripture warns that a divided house falls and commends the unity of brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: Short words of contempt spread quickly in wartime because they save a man from thinking about the person he is naming.
The church is called to a unity that politics cannot produce (Psa 133:1), and to put away the bitter speech that division breeds (Eph 4:31).
roots_summary: secession → clipped to secesh (OED earliest 1861).
roots_lines: 1860–1861: Southern states secede
1861: OED’s earliest evidence, Ohio Statesman
usage: "The Union soldiers’ letters called the town’s holdouts ‘the secesh.’"
And Jesus knew their thoughts, and said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand: (Mat 12:25).
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! (Psa 133:1).

etymology: An English compound of bush + whacker, per the Oxford English Dictionary. OED’s earliest evidence is from 1809, in the writing of Washington Irving, well before the war, and OED records the military sense from the 1860s. The American Battlefield Trust notes that in Missouri and the other border states guerrilla fighters of either side were commonly called bushwhackers.
biblical_def: A bushwhacker was a guerrilla who fought from cover, most famously in Missouri during the Civil War. The American Battlefield Trust records that guerrilla fighters of either side were commonly called bushwhackers in the border states. The word is older than the war and first described a backwoodsman who beat his way through the brush. The Christian observation: the bushwhacker’s method was the ambush, and Scripture names it for what it is. Wisdom’s first warning to a son is against the gang that says, "Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause" (Pro 1:11). The psalmist describes the wicked man who "sitteth in the lurking places of the villages" (Psa 10:8). Whatever the cause, God does not hand private men the sword of vengeance: "avenge not yourselves" (Rom 12:19).
webster_summary: A guerrilla who fights from ambush (OED from 1809; military sense 1860s); in the Civil War, the irregular raiders of the border states — the lurking that Scripture condemns (Pro 1:11; Psa 10:8).
webster_full: BUSHWHACKER, n. (from 1809, OED) 1. A backwoodsman. 2. (1860s, military) A guerrilla who fights from cover; in the Civil War, the irregular fighters of the border states (American Battlefield Trust).
scriptures: If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause:
He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor.
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: War waged from ambush on neighbors is murder by another name; Scripture warns sons away from the gang that lies in wait.
corruption_paragraphs: Guerrilla war blurs the line between soldier and civilian, and the border war in Missouri was cruel for exactly that reason.
Proverbs opens by warning young men against the band that lies in wait for blood (Pro 1:11). The warning still applies whenever violence is excused by a cause.
roots_summary: bush + whacker → backwoodsman (OED earliest 1809) → Civil War guerrilla of the border states (1860s).
roots_lines: 1809: OED’s earliest evidence, Washington Irving
1860s: OED records the military sense
1861–1865: guerrilla fighters of the border states, either side (American Battlefield Trust)
usage: "Union patrols in Missouri moved carefully through the timber for fear of bushwhackers."
If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause: (Pro 1:11).
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. (Rom 12:19).

etymology: From a proper name: Captain Charles Cunningham Boycott, an English land agent in County Mayo, Ireland. In 1880 his tenants and neighbours, organized under the Irish Land League, refused to work for him, sell to him, or deal with him at all. The Oxford English Dictionary dates both verb and noun to the 1880s.
biblical_def: To boycott is to refuse, together with others, to buy from, sell to, or deal with a person or business as a means of pressure. The word began with one man shut out by a whole countryside. Withholding trade is not sinful in itself: a Christian may lawfully decline to fund what he believes is wicked. But Scripture also shows the darker form, where the power to buy and sell is made to depend on loyalty to a ruling beast (Rev 13:17). The difference is whether conscience is being kept or coerced.
webster_summary: To refuse, in concert with others, all dealings with a person or business (OED 1880s, from Capt. Charles Boycott, Mayo, 1880); lawful as a matter of conscience, tyrannical when made a test of allegiance (Rev 13:17).
webster_full: BOYCOTT, v. (from 1880s, OED) To combine in refusing commercial or social dealings with a person, group, or business, as a means of protest or coercion.
n. The act or practice of boycotting. From Capt. Charles C. Boycott (1832–1897), land agent ostracized in County Mayo, 1880.
scriptures: And that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.
corruption_summary: A boycott can be an act of conscience or an act of coercion; the age tends to praise the one it agrees with and condemn the other, without asking which is which.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern campaign to cut a person off from employment, banking, or trade for holding the wrong opinion is a boycott in its harshest form. It does not persuade; it punishes until the conscience yields.

Scripture gives the Christian freedom to keep his hands clean, and it also warns of a day when buying and selling will be made to hang on a mark of allegiance (Rev 13:17). The first is stewardship; the second is tyranny over the conscience.
roots_summary: Proper name Boycott → Mayo land agent shut out by the Land League (1880) → boycott, verb and noun (OED 1880s).
roots_lines: 1880: Capt. Charles C. Boycott ostracized by tenants and tradesmen in County Mayo, Ireland
1880s: OED’s earliest evidence for both verb and noun
Today: any concerted refusal to trade or deal
usage: "The family decided to boycott the store after it began selling what they would not bring home."
And that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name. (Rev 13:17).

etymology: From a proper name: James Thomas Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan (1797–1868), the British cavalry officer who led the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava in the Crimean War (25 October 1854). The knitted woollen jacket was named for him. The Oxford English Dictionary dates the word to the 1850s.
biblical_def: A cardigan is a knitted jacket or sweater that opens down the front. It carries the name of a cavalry earl from the Crimean War, so an everyday garment remembers a battlefield. Scripture takes ordinary clothing seriously too. Near the end of his life, in prison, Paul asked Timothy to bring "the cloke that I left at Troas" (2Ti 4:13). The apostle needed a warm coat and his books, and he was not ashamed to say so.
webster_summary: A knitted jacket opening down the front (OED 1850s), named for the 7th Earl of Cardigan of the Light Brigade; an ordinary garment, as ordinary as Paul’s cloke (2Ti 4:13).
webster_full: CARDIGAN, n. (from 1850s, OED) A knitted woollen jacket or sweater, usually buttoned down the front. From the 7th Earl of Cardigan (1797–1868).
scriptures: The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments.
corruption_summary: No moral corruption attaches to the word; the only loss is memory, since few who wear one know it once honoured a Crimean cavalry commander.
corruption_paragraphs: Words like cardigan carry history quietly. The garment kept its name long after the man and the charge were forgotten.
The plain point is that God cares for ordinary needs. Paul asked for his coat as well as his parchments (2Ti 4:13), and the Lord who clothes the grass of the field knows what His people need.
roots_summary: Proper name Cardigan (7th Earl) → Crimean War, 1854 → cardigan, knitted jacket (OED 1850s).
roots_lines: 25 October 1854: Lord Cardigan leads the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava
1850s: OED’s earliest evidence for cardigan as a garment
usage: "He put on his old cardigan and sat down with the Bible."
The cloke that I left at Troas with Carpus, when thou comest, bring with thee, and the books, but especially the parchments. (2Ti 4:13).

etymology: From a proper name: Henry Shrapnel (1761–1842), an officer of the British Royal Artillery who devised a hollow shell filled with musket balls and a bursting charge, timed to break open over enemy troops. The British Army adopted it in 1803. The Oxford English Dictionary dates shrapnel to the 1800s; it later came to mean any fragments thrown out by an exploding shell or bomb.
biblical_def: Shrapnel is the metal scattered by an exploding shell. The word began as the name of an artillery officer and his invention, and it now names one of the commonest wounds of modern war. Scripture does not pretend war is clean. It also promises that the Lord will one day bring it to an end: "He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder" (Psa 46:9).
webster_summary: Fragments thrown by an exploding shell, from Henry Shrapnel’s shell adopted 1803 (OED 1800s); the wound of modern war, which the Lord will end (Psa 46:9).
webster_full: SHRAPNEL, n. (from 1800s, OED) Originally a shell containing bullets and a charge to burst it in flight; now, fragments of a shell, bomb, or mine. From Henry Shrapnel (1761–1842), Royal Artillery.
scriptures: He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
corruption_summary: None in the word itself; the danger is the familiarity that lets a civilian age forget what shrapnel does to a body.
corruption_paragraphs: Every Marine and soldier who has heard the word in earnest knows it is not abstract. A nation that sends men to war owes them honesty about the cost.
The Christian holds two truths together: the magistrate bears the sword lawfully, and the Lord will break the bow and the spear at the last (Psa 46:9).
roots_summary: Proper name Shrapnel → spherical case shot adopted 1803 → shrapnel (OED 1800s) → any shell fragments.
roots_lines: 1803: British Army adopts Henry Shrapnel’s shell
1800s: OED’s earliest evidence for shrapnel
20th century: the word widens to mean any fragments from an explosion
usage: "The corpsman pulled a piece of shrapnel from his arm."
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire. (Psa 46:9).

etymology: From a proper name: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718–1792). The Oxford English Dictionary dates the food sense to the mid 1700s. The familiar story that the earl called for meat between slices of bread so he need not leave the gaming table comes from a French visitor’s account and cannot be confirmed; the name itself is not in doubt.
biblical_def: A sandwich is food laid between two pieces of bread. It is the plainest of meals, named for an English earl. The Christian observation is simple: bread is still the gift of God. Our Lord taught us to ask for it one day at a time: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Mat 6:11). The man who eats a sandwich at his desk is no less dependent on that petition than Israel was on manna.
webster_summary: Food between two slices of bread (OED mid 1700s), named for the 4th Earl of Sandwich; plain daily bread, asked of God (Mat 6:11).
webster_full: SANDWICH, n. (from mid 1700s, OED) Two or more slices of bread with a filling between them. From John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich (1718–1792).
The gaming-table story is popular but unproven; the proper-name origin is attested.
scriptures: Give us this day our daily bread.
corruption_summary: The word is innocent; what the age forgets is the One who gives the bread.
corruption_paragraphs: Abundance makes a meal routine, and routine makes thanksgiving rare. The quickest meal is still a gift.
Whether we eat or drink, Scripture calls us to give thanks to God by Christ (Col 3:17).
roots_summary: Proper name Sandwich (4th Earl) → sandwich, food between bread (OED mid 1700s).
roots_lines: 1718–1792: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich
Mid 1700s: OED’s earliest evidence for the food sense
Gaming-table anecdote: popular, unconfirmed
usage: "We prayed over the sandwiches before the hike."
Give us this day our daily bread. (Mat 6:11).

etymology: From a proper name: Samuel Augustus Maverick (1803–1870), a Texas lawyer and landowner and a signer of the Texas Declaration of Independence, who did not brand his calves. Unbranded cattle on the range came to be called mavericks. The Oxford English Dictionary dates the word to the 1860s, with the political sense of an independent who will not run with the herd from the 1880s.
biblical_def: A maverick was first an unbranded calf, belonging to no visible owner. It now means a person who goes his own way. Independence can be courage, and it can be pride. Scripture’s picture is the flock that is known by name: "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine" (Joh 10:14). The Christian is never truly unbranded. The question is whose he is.
webster_summary: An unbranded calf, from Samuel Maverick of Texas (OED 1860s); now an independent. The believer is not unowned but known by the Good Shepherd (Joh 10:14).
webster_full: MAVERICK, n. (from 1860s, OED) An unbranded calf or yearling. 2. (from 1880s) A person, especially a politician, who refuses to follow the party or herd. From Samuel A. Maverick (1803–1870).
scriptures: I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine.
corruption_summary: The age makes the maverick a hero simply for refusing to belong; Scripture asks first whether the independence is obedience to God or rebellion against Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Standing alone is right when the herd is wrong. Daniel, Elijah, and the Reformers all stood alone. But independence is not a virtue in itself; the Proverbs warn often against the man who is wise in his own eyes.
The Christian answer is ownership, not autonomy. He has been bought with a price and belongs to the Shepherd who knows him (Joh 10:14).
roots_summary: Proper name Maverick → unbranded Texas calves → maverick (OED 1860s) → political independent (1880s).
roots_lines: 1803–1870: Samuel A. Maverick, Texas
1860s: OED’s earliest evidence (cattle)
1880s: political sense
usage: "He was a maverick in the legislature, and he voted his conscience."
I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine. (Joh 10:14).

etymology: From a proper name, with the suffix -ize: Thomas Bowdler (1754–1825), who published The Family Shakspeare, an edition of Shakespeare with passages he judged unfit for family reading removed. The Oxford English Dictionary dates bowdlerize to the 1830s.
biblical_def: To bowdlerize is to cut from a text whatever an editor finds offensive, leaving a weaker book that still carries the author’s name. With Shakespeare it is a question of taste. With the Word of God it is a grave sin. The last chapter of the Bible warns: "if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life" (Rev 22:19). No editor may improve on Scripture by cutting it.
webster_summary: To expurgate a text by removing what is judged offensive (OED 1830s), from Thomas Bowdler’s Family Shakspeare; forbidden toward Scripture (Rev 22:19).
webster_full: BOWDLERIZE, v. (from 1830s, OED) To remove material considered improper or offensive from a book; to expurgate, often so as to weaken it. From Thomas Bowdler (1754–1825).
scriptures: And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book.
corruption_summary: Modern bowdlerizing runs the other way from Bowdler: it cuts the hard words of Scripture on sin, judgment, and the sexes because they offend the age.
corruption_paragraphs: Bowdler removed coarse words from a play. Modern preaching often removes hell, wrath, repentance, and the order of creation from the Bible, while still claiming to preach the Bible.
The warning of Rev 22:19 is not about taste. A church that keeps the comfortable verses and quietly drops the rest has bowdlerized the Word of God.
roots_summary: Proper name Bowdler + -ize → bowdlerize (OED 1830s).
roots_lines: 1754–1825: Thomas Bowdler, editor of The Family Shakspeare
1830s: OED’s earliest evidence for bowdlerize
usage: "A sermon that skips judgment has bowdlerized the text."

And if any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life, and out of the holy city, and from the things which are written in this book. (Rev 22:19).

etymology: From a proper name: Étienne de Silhouette (1709–1767), Controller-General of Finances in France in 1759, whose severe economies made his name a byword for anything cheap or bare. The outline portrait cut from dark paper took his name. The Oxford English Dictionary dates the English word to the late 1700s.
biblical_def: A silhouette is an outline filled in with a single dark tone, the shape of a thing without its detail. Scripture uses the same idea for the law of Moses: "the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things" (Heb 10:1). The sacrifices gave the outline; Christ is the substance. A silhouette is real, but it points past itself.
webster_summary: A dark outline portrait or shape (OED late 1700s), from Étienne de Silhouette; like the law, a shadow of good things to come, not the very image (Heb 10:1).
webster_full: SILHOUETTE, n. (from late 1700s, OED) A portrait or picture showing only the outline, filled in black; any dark outline seen against a lighter background. From Étienne de Silhouette (1709–1767).
scriptures: For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.
corruption_summary: No moral corruption attaches to the word; it is a useful picture of shadow and substance.
corruption_paragraphs: The error to avoid is staying with the shadow when the substance has come. Hebrews warns against returning to the outlines of the old covenant after Christ has fulfilled them.
The silhouette honours the shape; only the person fills it in. So the law honours Christ, and only Christ fulfils it (Heb 10:1).
roots_summary: Proper name Silhouette (Controller-General, 1759) → silhouette, outline portrait (OED late 1700s).
roots_lines: 1759: Étienne de Silhouette, French Controller-General of Finances
Late 1700s: OED’s earliest evidence in English
usage: "The steeple stood in silhouette against the sunset."

For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect. (Heb 10:1).

etymology: A blend of a proper name and salamander. In 1812 the Massachusetts legislature, under Governor Elbridge Gerry, redrew a state senate district into a shape that critics said looked like a salamander, and the Gerry-mander was born. The Oxford English Dictionary dates the word to the 1810s. Gerry pronounced his name with a hard G; the word is now usually said with a soft one.
biblical_def: To gerrymander is to draw election districts to secure an advantage for one party. It is the electoral version of a false balance: the votes are counted honestly, but the scale was rigged before anyone voted. Scripture’s standard for every measure applies: "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight" (Pro 11:1). A just magistrate draws just lines.
webster_summary: Manipulating district boundaries for partisan advantage (OED 1810s), from Gov. Elbridge Gerry + salamander, 1812; a false balance (Pro 11:1).
webster_full: GERRYMANDER, n. (from 1810s, OED) An arrangement of electoral districts made to give one party an unfair advantage. v. To draw districts so. From Elbridge Gerry (1744–1814), governor of Massachusetts, + salamander.
scriptures: A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
corruption_summary: Every party condemns the other side’s gerrymander and calls its own fair; Scripture’s just weight binds both.
corruption_paragraphs: Gerrymandering is old, legal in many forms, and practised by both parties. That makes it common, not right.
The magistrate is a minister of God for good (Rom 13:4), and a rigged scale is an abomination to the LORD (Pro 11:1), whoever holds it.
roots_summary: Proper name Gerry + salamander → Gerry-mander (Massachusetts, 1812) → gerrymander (OED 1810s).
roots_lines: 1812: Massachusetts senate districts redrawn under Gov. Elbridge Gerry
1810s: OED’s earliest evidence
usage: "The new map gerrymandered our county into three pieces."
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight. (Pro 11:1).

etymology: From a proper name: Vidkun Quisling (1887–1945), the Norwegian Nazi party leader who proclaimed himself head of government on the day Germany invaded Norway in April 1940 and later served as head of the occupation government. He was tried and executed for treason in October 1945. The Oxford English Dictionary dates quisling, a traitor who collaborates with an occupying enemy, to the 1940s.
biblical_def: A quisling is a traitor who helps an invader rule his own people. The word was coined within days of the betrayal that gave it its name. Scripture knows this sin intimately. David wrote of it, and our Lord applied the words to Judas: "mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me" (Psa 41:9).
webster_summary: A traitor who collaborates with an occupying enemy (OED 1940s), from Vidkun Quisling of Norway, 1940; the treachery of the familiar friend (Psa 41:9).
webster_full: QUISLING, n. (from 1940s, OED) A traitor who collaborates with an enemy occupying his country. From Vidkun Quisling (1887–1945).
scriptures: Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
corruption_summary: The word is sometimes thrown at mere opponents; it belongs to real treachery, and its force depends on keeping it there.
corruption_paragraphs: Calling every political rival a traitor cheapens the charge until it means nothing. Quisling sold his country to an invading army; that is the measure.
The worst treachery in history was from a friend at table (Psa 41:9). The Christian guards his own loyalties before he names anyone else a quisling.
roots_summary: Proper name Quisling → Norway, April 1940 → quisling, collaborator (OED 1940s).
roots_lines: 9 April 1940: Germany invades Norway; Quisling proclaims himself head of government
October 1945: executed for treason
1940s: OED’s earliest evidence
usage: "The resistance knew who the quislings were."
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me. (Psa 41:9).

etymology: From a proper name: Jules Léotard (1838–1870), the French acrobat who introduced the flying trapeze act in Paris in 1859 and performed in a close-fitting one-piece garment. The Oxford English Dictionary dates leotard to the 1920s.
biblical_def: A leotard is a close-fitting one-piece garment worn for gymnastics, dance, and exercise. It is named for a trapeze performer. Scripture gives bodily training its true place: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). Paul does not despise the body; he ranks its training below the training of the soul.
webster_summary: A close-fitting one-piece garment for exercise (OED 1920s), from trapeze artist Jules Léotard; bodily exercise has its place, godliness the greater (1Ti 4:8).
webster_full: LEOTARD, n. (from 1920s, OED) A close-fitting one-piece garment covering the torso, worn by dancers, gymnasts, and acrobats. From Jules Léotard (1838–1870).
scriptures: For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
corruption_summary: No moral corruption attaches to the word; the error it can serve is a culture that trains the body and neglects the soul.
corruption_paragraphs: An age devoted to fitness can spend hours on the body and minutes on prayer. Paul reverses the priority without despising exercise.
Godliness has promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come (1Ti 4:8).
roots_summary: Proper name Léotard → flying trapeze, Paris, 1859 → leotard (OED 1920s).
roots_lines: 1859: Jules Léotard performs the first flying trapeze act
1920s: OED’s earliest evidence for leotard
usage: "Her gymnastics leotard was hung by the door."
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come. (1Ti 4:8).

etymology: From a proper name: Rudolf Diesel (1858–1913), the German engineer who patented the compression-ignition engine in the 1890s. In 1913 he disappeared overboard from a steamer crossing to England. The Oxford English Dictionary dates diesel to the 1890s.
biblical_def: A diesel is an engine that ignites its fuel by the heat of compressed air, or the fuel that runs it. It carries the name of a diligent engineer whose invention now moves ships, trains, and trucks. Scripture honours that kind of skill: "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). Good work, well done, serves neighbours far beyond the workshop.
webster_summary: A compression-ignition engine or its fuel (OED 1890s), from engineer Rudolf Diesel; skilled diligence that serves many (Pro 22:29).
webster_full: DIESEL, n. (from 1890s, OED) An internal-combustion engine in which fuel is ignited by the heat of compressed air; the fuel for such an engine. From Rudolf Diesel (1858–1913).
scriptures: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
corruption_summary: No moral corruption attaches to the word.
corruption_paragraphs: Engineering is a calling, not merely a career. The man who designs an engine that hauls a nation’s food is serving his neighbour.
Whatever is done in word or deed is to be done in the name of the Lord Jesus (Col 3:17).
roots_summary: Proper name Diesel → compression-ignition engine (1890s) → diesel, engine and fuel (OED 1890s).
roots_lines: 1890s: Rudolf Diesel patents his engine; OED’s earliest evidence
1913: Diesel lost overboard crossing to England
usage: "The old farm truck still runs on diesel."
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men. (Pro 22:29).

etymology: From a proper name: Derrick, a hangman at Tyburn in London around 1600. His name was first given to the gallows itself, and from there to a hoisting apparatus with a beam, and later to the framework over an oil well. The Oxford English Dictionary dates derrick to the early 1600s.
biblical_def: A derrick is a crane or the tower over a drilling well. Its first meaning was a gallows, named for a London executioner. A word for hanging became a word for lifting. Scripture contains the deepest form of that reversal: "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (Gal 3:13). The tree of the curse became the means of lifting sinners up.
webster_summary: A crane or well tower; first a gallows, from the Tyburn hangman Derrick (OED early 1600s); the tree of the curse turned to lifting (Gal 3:13).
webster_full: DERRICK, n. (from early 1600s, OED) 1. A hangman; the gallows (obsolete). 2. A hoisting apparatus with a boom. 3. The framework over an oil well or drill hole. From Derrick, hangman at Tyburn, c. 1600.
scriptures: Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
corruption_summary: No moral corruption attaches to the word; the forgotten history is that of the gallows.
corruption_paragraphs: Few men on a drilling rig know they work under a word for a hangman. The history is grim, but it is honest.
The cross was a gallows too, and Christ was made a curse upon it so that we might be redeemed (Gal 3:13).
roots_summary: Proper name Derrick (Tyburn hangman) → gallows (early 1600s) → crane → oil derrick.
roots_lines: c. 1600: Derrick, hangman at Tyburn
Early 1600s: OED’s earliest evidence (hangman, gallows)
Later: hoisting apparatus; framework over an oil well
usage: "The derrick stood over the well like a steeple."
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree: (Gal 3:13).

etymology: From a proper name combined with Greek: Adolphe Sax (1814–1894), the Belgian instrument maker who patented the instrument in Paris in 1846, + Greek -phonos, “sounding.” The Oxford English Dictionary dates saxophone to the 1850s.
biblical_def: A saxophone is a single-reed wind instrument of brass, named for its inventor. Like every instrument, it can be used well or badly. The Psalms call God’s people to praise Him with many instruments: "Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs" (Psa 150:4), and to "play skilfully" (Psa 33:3). Skill offered to God is worship; skill offered to self is display.
webster_summary: A single-reed brass wind instrument (OED 1850s), from Adolphe Sax + Greek -phonos; instruments to be played skilfully unto the Lord (Psa 33:3; Psa 150:4).
webster_full: SAXOPHONE, n. (from 1850s, OED) A wind instrument of brass with a single reed and finger keys. From Adolphe Sax (1814–1894) + Greek -phonos, sounding.
scriptures: Praise him with the timbrel and dance: praise him with stringed instruments and organs.
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise.
corruption_summary: No moral corruption attaches to the word; the question is always what the music serves.
corruption_paragraphs: Instruments are not holy or unholy in themselves. The heart and the aim of the player decide whether music honours God.
Scripture asks for skill (Psa 33:3) and for praise directed to Him (Psa 150:4), not to the performer.
roots_summary: Proper name Sax + Greek -phonos → saxophone (patented 1846; OED 1850s).
roots_lines: 1846: Adolphe Sax patents the saxophone in Paris
1850s: OED’s earliest evidence in English
usage: "The saxophone carried the melody of the old hymn."
Sing unto him a new song; play skilfully with a loud noise. (Psa 33:3).

etymology: A borrowing from Italian fascista, a member of a fascio, “bundle” or political group, from Latin fasces, the bundle of rods bound around an axe carried before Roman magistrates as a sign of their authority. Benito Mussolini founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in Milan in March 1919. The Oxford English Dictionary dates fascist in English to the 1910s.
biblical_def: A fascist, in the word’s real sense, is an adherent of the movement Mussolini founded in 1919 and of the ideas it shared with related regimes: a nation gathered into a single all-embracing state, ruled by one party and one leader, with no sphere of life outside its claim. Scripture rejects that claim at the root. The magistrate is “the minister of God” (Rom 13:4); he is under God, not in God’s place, and family, church, and conscience are not his property. That is the word’s meaning. The ninth commandment governs how it may be used: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour" (Exo 20:16).
webster_summary: A member or adherent of Mussolini’s movement (1919) or a like totalizing nationalist regime (OED 1910s; Italian fascista, from fascio, Latin fasces); now widely used as a loose epithet for any opponent.
webster_full: FASCIST, n. and adj. (from 1910s, OED) A member of the Italian Fascist party founded by Mussolini in 1919; an adherent of fascism, an authoritarian nationalist system in which the state claims every sphere of life. Italian fascista, from fascio, bundle, group; Latin fasces.
Orwell observed in 1946 (“Politics and the English Language”) that the word had already come to mean little more than “something not desirable.”
scriptures: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
corruption_summary: Fascist is now hurled at parents, pastors, and ordinary voters who hold Christian convictions, emptied of its historical content and used to end argument rather than make one.
corruption_paragraphs: The word names a real system with a real history: one party, one leader, and a state that claims everything. That system is worth naming accurately, because it is a genuine enemy of the church and the family. When the label is stretched to cover anyone who opposes a progressive cause, it stops describing anything. George Orwell saw this already in 1946, when he wrote that the word had come to mean only “something not desirable.”

In current use it is often applied to the very people who resist the state’s claim over the home and the conscience: parents objecting to school curricula, churches refusing state orders, citizens defending limited government. That is calling evil good and good evil (Isa 5:20). An accusation of this weight, made without evidence, is false witness against a neighbour (Exo 20:16), and every idle word will be accounted for in the day of judgment (Mat 12:36).

The Christian answer is twofold. Use the word accurately, and only of what it actually means. And when it is thrown at you, answer with facts and a quiet conscience, since “he that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17).
roots_summary: Latin fasces (rods and axe of Roman authority) → Italian fascio (bundle, group) → fascista (Mussolini’s movement, 1919) → English fascist (OED 1910s) → loose modern epithet.
roots_lines: Latin fasces: bundle of rods around an axe, emblem of Roman magistrates
March 1919: Fasci Italiani di Combattimento founded in Milan
1910s: OED’s earliest evidence for English fascist
1946: Orwell notes the word has come to mean “something not desirable”
usage: "Calling the school board ‘fascists’ for hearing parents is not an argument."
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour. (Exo 20:16).
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter! (Isa 5:20).
